title: Financial Fraud and Scams
summary: Pause, verify, protect, report and recover: a calm routine for when a scammer calls.
subtitle: Slow the scam down before it speeds your money away

blocks.text: A scammer’s favourite financial product is urgency. It has no prospectus, no cooling-off period and apparently comes with unlimited exclamation marks.

Fraud can arrive as a bank alert, a fake government call, romance, an investment pitch, a job offer, a marketplace buyer, a family emergency or a recovery service. The costume changes. The pressure pattern often repeats. This drill teaches a response you can repeat, without blaming the person targeted. Skilled fraudsters use emotion, timing, trusted names and realistic technology to get past ordinary judgment.
A caller ID, email logo or familiar-looking website is not proof of identity. End the contact and verify through a phone number or website you locate independently.

items.title: “Only careless people fall for scams.”
items.text: Fraud is built to exploit trust, fear, hope, authority and time pressure. Anyone can be targeted. A rehearsed pause and check routine is more useful than shame.

blocks.text: A five-question scan is what separates a real emergency from a rehearsed one.
blocks.detail: Running the same five checks every time is what turns a racing pulse back into a decision.
blocks.extra: Meet Colin next, mid-call, with the potatoes still boiling.

blocks.text: Use the STOP test. Source: did you start the contact? Time: are you being rushed? Offer: does the claim hold up to an independent check? Payment: does the method remove your usual protections? One red flag does not prove fraud, but it earns a pause.

items.text: Source: did you start the contact through a channel you trust?
Time: are you being rushed, threatened or told to keep the request secret?
Offer: does the claim survive an independent check?
Payment: does the requested method remove your usual protections?
Credentials: are you being asked for a password, PIN, one-time code, remote access or card pickup?

blocks.text: One-time passcodes are keys, not customer-service trivia. A legitimate code arriving on your device can still be part of a fraudster’s login attempt. Never read it to an unsolicited caller.

items.title: “If the caller knows my name, bank and recent details, the call is genuine.”
items.text: Personal details can come from data breaches, social media, stolen mail or an earlier contact. Check independently, and never trust a caller just because they know things about you.

sections.title: Colin, the Bank Investigator and the Very Helpful Courier

paragraphs: Colin Fraser is making supper in Winnipeg when his phone shows the name of his bank. The caller knows his full name. He says the fraud department has spotted a transfer. To protect Colin’s savings, he must move the money into a ‘secure account’ before the branch closes. The caller is calm, careful and impressively concerned.

Then a real one-time code arrives by text. The caller asks Colin to read it aloud. Next he says a courier will collect Colin’s bank card as evidence. Colin feels embarrassed that he is unsure. The potatoes are boiling over, the caller is counting down and the whole evening has become a low-budget thriller with excellent caller ID.

Colin remembers a family rule: no money, code or card leaves during an incoming contact. He hangs up, even though the caller warns that the transfer will become permanent. He calls the number on the back of his card. The bank says it never called, and it locks the attempted login. Colin changes his password from a clean device. He checks his recent transactions and turns on stronger multi-factor authentication.

He saves the phone number, the text, the time and his notes without clicking anything. He follows the bank’s instructions. He reports the call to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and tells local police as needed. He also tells his sister, who got a similar call that week.

Two days later, someone offers to recover money for an upfront fee. Colin has lost no money, but this second caller has plenty of optimism and an invoice ready. Colin refuses and adds the contact to his report. He did not outsmart every scam. He used a routine that works under stress: pause, leave the channel, verify, protect and report.

blocks.text: Recovery scams often target people who were already contacted or harmed. A caller who knows details from the first incident does not prove they are a real recovery service. Check independently, and never send an upfront payment under pressure.
Colin used a family rule he had decided in advance, a trusted way to reach the bank and fast account protection. The routine broke the pressure cycle. Perfect confidence did not.
Colin's rule cost him nothing and saved his account, because he had decided it before he ever needed it.
blocks.detail: Building a household response ladder now is what keeps a future call short instead of expensive.
blocks.extra: Build your own response card next, before the phone rings.

items.title: Protect safety
items.text: If anyone is in danger, call 911. Do not meet a courier, confront a suspect or keep talking to collect evidence.

items.title: Contact the money channel
items.text: Call the bank, card issuer, payment service, crypto platform or transfer provider right away, using a trusted number. Ask about stopping, recalling, freezing or disputing the payment.

items.title: Secure access
items.text: Change exposed passwords from a trusted device, starting with email and financial accounts. Turn on MFA and follow the provider's instructions.

items.title: Preserve evidence
items.text: Keep receipts, transaction IDs, messages, numbers, profiles, websites, dates and a short timeline. Do not leave suspicious software open just to take a better screenshot.

items.title: Report and update
items.text: Report fraud or attempted fraud to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. Report to local police when appropriate, and get a file number. Update the report if new activity appears.

blocks.text: Reporting an attempted scam still matters. It can connect patterns, warn others and support investigations even when no money left your account.
Preserve facts, not shame: what contact arrived, what was shared, what moved, when it happened and what protection followed.

items.title: “Once money is sent, reporting is pointless.”
items.text: Recovery is not guaranteed, but acting fast may improve the chance of stopping or tracing a payment. Reporting also creates records that help investigators. Act quickly, and beware anyone promising recovery for an upfront fee.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is a separate channel essential for verification?
items.detail: You leave the suspicious contact and reach the real organization through contact details you found yourself.

items.title: Name three pressure signals that justify a pause.
items.detail: Rushing, secrecy, threats, someone pretending to be someone else, odd payment methods or requests for codes and passwords.

items.title: What should you do with an unexpected one-time passcode request?
items.detail: Do not share it. End the contact and verify independently.

items.title: What are the first two organizations to contact after money is transferred fraudulently?
items.detail: The bank or payment provider right away, then local police or the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre as needed.

items.title: Why report attempted fraud and recovery scams?
items.detail: Reports connect patterns, warn others, support investigations and document follow-up activity.

sections.title: Your Action: Household Scam Response Card

blocks.text: Write down who to contact, not passwords, PINs, one-time codes, full card numbers or security answers.
A household code phrase can confirm a real family emergency request. Confirm it through another known contact, and do not let an urgent voice message appoint itself chief financial officer.
Urgency is the signal to slow down, not speed up.
blocks.detail: Pause on incoming requests, check through a separate trusted channel, protect accounts quickly and report the facts without shame. A rehearsed routine works better than perfect confidence.

items.title: Phishing
items.text: A fake message or site meant to trick you into giving up information, money or access.

items.title: Spoofing
items.text: Faking the caller, sender or website details you see, to look trustworthy.

items.title: Social engineering
items.text: Tricking people through emotion, trust or pressure, not just through technical attacks.

items.title: One-time passcode
items.text: A temporary code used to confirm access or a payment. Do not share it with anyone who contacts you out of the blue.

items.title: Recovery scam
items.text: A follow-up fraud that promises to get your money back, often for an upfront fee.

items.title: MFA
items.text: Multi-factor authentication: more than one type of proof is needed to open an account.

quiz.question: True or False: “Only careless people fall for scams.”

questions: What is your household’s rule for any request for money, codes or passwords that comes in by call, text or email?
Where will you keep the trusted phone numbers or bookmarked sites for your bank and cards?
Which two people will you call for a quick pause-and-check, and what red flags will make you stop?
Which accounts need a unique password and stronger MFA? Start with email and banking.
If you were scammed, what would you save as evidence, and who would you contact first?
When will you hold a 10-minute scam drill with your household?
